title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
authors:
Alec Radford, Jong Wook Kim, Chris Hallacy, Aditya Ramesh, Gabriel
  Goh, Sandhini Agarwal, Girish Sastry, Amanda Askell, Pamela Mishkin, Jack
  Clark, Gretchen Krueger, Ilya Sutskever
reason: Introduced the CLIP architecture and the contrastive language-image pre-training objective, which is the basis for modern VLMs.
summary: Traditional computer vision models are limited by fixed object categories and require task-specific labeled data to recognize new concepts. Researchers trained a model on 400 million image-text pairs from the internet by predicting which captions match which images, allowing it to understand visual concepts through natural language. This approach enables zero-shot transfer to new tasks, matching the accuracy of a supervised ResNet-50 on ImageNet without any task-specific training.

title:
BLIP-2: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training with Frozen Image
  Encoders and Large Language Models
authors: Junnan Li, Dongxu Li, Silvio Savarese, Steven Hoi
reason: Introduces the Q-Former architecture and a two-stage bootstrapping objective, which are central to modern efficient VLM design.
summary: To reduce the high computational costs of vision-language pre-training, the authors propose BLIP-2, a method that uses a lightweight Querying Transformer to bridge frozen, pre-trained image encoders and large language models. The strategy employs a two-stage training process to learn vision-language representations and vision-to-language generation. BLIP-2 achieves state-of-the-art results, including outperforming Flamingo80B by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2 while using 54x fewer trainable parameters.

title: Visual Instruction Tuning
authors: Haotian Liu, Chunyuan Li, Qingyang Wu, Yong Jae Lee
reason: Introduced the LLaVA architecture and the paradigm of visual instruction tuning, which is a central method for modern VLMs.
summary: This paper addresses the lack of multimodal instruction-following data by using GPT-4 to generate language-image instruction datasets for training. The researchers developed LLaVA, an end-to-end model that connects a vision encoder to a large language model, to enable general-purpose visual and language understanding. LLaVA achieved 85.1% of GPT-4's performance on a synthetic multimodal dataset and, when combined with GPT-4 for Science QA, reached a state-of-the-art accuracy of 92.53%.

The resulting model achieves new state-of-the-art performance in few-shot learning across various visual question-answering and captioning benchmarks, outperforming models fine-tuned on thousands of times more task-specific data.

title:

  Vision-Language Understanding and Generation
authors: Junnan Li, Dongxu Li, Caiming Xiong, Steven Hoi
reason: Introduces a key unified architecture and bootstrapping objective (captioner/filter) that bridges understanding and generation in VLMs.
summary: Existing vision-language models often struggle to perform both understanding and generation tasks effectively while suffering from noisy web-scale datasets. This method achieves state-of-the-art results, including a 2.7% increase in average recall@1 for image-text retrieval and a 2.8% improvement in CIDEr for image captioning.

title: Improved Baselines with Visual Instruction Tuning
authors: Haotian Liu, Chunyuan Li, Yuheng Li, Yong Jae Lee
reason: Establishes the standard architecture (CLIP + MLP projection + LLM) and instruction-tuning paradigm used in most modern LMMs.

title:
An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at
  Scale
authors:

summary: Current computer vision models rely heavily on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) rather than using the Transformer architecture directly on image data. The researchers developed the Vision Transformer (ViT), which applies a pure Transformer architecture to sequences of image patches instead of using convolutions. When pre-trained on large datasets, ViT achieves state-of-the-art results on various image recognition benchmarks while requiring significantly fewer computational resources to train.

title: Sigmoid Loss for Language Image Pre-Training
authors: Xiaohua Zhai, Basil Mustafa, Alexander Kolesnikov, Lucas Beyer
reason: Introduces SigLIP, a major alternative to CLIP's softmax loss that is now a standard training objective for modern VLMs.
summary: Standard contrastive language-image pre-training relies on softmax normalization, which requires a global view of all pairs and limits batch size scalability. The researchers propose SigLIP, a pairwise sigmoid loss that treats each image-text pair independently, allowing for easier scaling and better performance at smaller batch sizes. Using this method with Locked-image Tuning, they achieved 84.5% ImageNet zero-shot accuracy in just two days using only four TPUv4 chips.

title:
Scaling Up Visual and Vision-Language Representation Learning With Noisy
  Text Supervision
authors:

reason: Describes the scaling of dual-encoder architectures and contrastive loss using massive noisy datasets, a central pillar of modern VLMs.
summary: To overcome the high cost of curating high-quality vision-language datasets, this research utilizes a massive, uncurated dataset of over one billion noisy image-alt-text pairs. The authors employ a simple dual-encoder architecture trained with a contrastive loss to align visual and linguistic representations. This large-scale approach achieves state-of-the-art results on image-text retrieval benchmarks like Flickr30K and MSCOCO, while also providing strong performance in zero-shot image classification.

title: CoCa: Contrastive Captioners are Image-Text Foundation Models
authors:

reason: A key architecture that unifies contrastive (CLIP-style) and generative (captioning) objectives, central to modern VLM design.
summary: CoCa addresses the need for a unified foundation model by combining the strengths of contrastive learning (like CLIP) and generative captioning (like SimVLM) into a single architecture. The method uses an encoder-decoder transformer trained simultaneously with contrastive and captioning losses to learn both image-text embeddings and autoregressive text generation. This approach achieves state-of-the-art results across various tasks, including a top-1 ImageNet accuracy of 91.0% when the encoder is fine-tuned.

title:
ViLBERT: Pretraining Task-Agnostic Visiolinguistic Representations for
  Vision-and-Language Tasks
authors: Jiasen Lu, Dhruv Batra, Devi Parikh, Stefan Lee
reason: Introduced the two-stream co-attention transformer architecture and pretraining paradigm that defined early modern VLM development.
summary: To learn joint representations of images and text, the researchers developed ViLBERT, a two-stream transformer model that processes visual and textual inputs separately and interacts them via co-attentional layers. The model was pretrained on the Conceptual Captions dataset using two proxy tasks and then transferred to various vision-and-language applications. ViLBERT achieved state-of-the-art results across four major tasks: visual question answering, visual commonsense reasoning, referring expressions, and caption-based image retrieval.

title: UNITER: UNiversal Image-TExt Representation Learning
authors:
Yen-Chun Chen, Linjie Li, Licheng Yu, Ahmed El Kholy, Faisal Ahmed,

reason: A key early architecture and pre-training framework (MLM, ITM, WRA) that established the standard for joint vision-language representation learning.
summary: UNITER addresses the need for a universal joint image-text embedding to power diverse vision-and-language tasks. The researchers pre-trained a model on four large-scale datasets using four specific tasks: Masked Language Modeling, Masked Region Modeling, Image-Text Matching, and a new Word-Region Alignment task based on Optimal Transport. This approach achieved new state-of-the-art results across six different vision-and-language tasks on over nine datasets.

title:
Align before Fuse: Vision and Language Representation Learning with
  Momentum Distillation
authors:
Junnan Li, Ramprasaath R. Selvaraju, Akhilesh Deepak Gotmare, Shafiq

reason: Introduces the 'align before fuse' paradigm (contrastive pre-training before multimodal fusion), a key architectural/objective pattern in VLMs.
summary: Existing multimodal encoders struggle to learn image-text interactions because visual and word tokens are unaligned before fusion. The researchers propose ALBEF, which uses a contrastive loss to align representations before cross-modal attention and employs momentum distillation to learn from noisy web data. This method achieves state-of-the-art results, including absolute improvements of 2.37% on VQA and 3.84% on NLVR$^2$ compared to previous models.

title: Attention Is All You Need
authors:
Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion

reason: The Transformer architecture is the fundamental building block for nearly all modern vision-language models (e.g., ViT, CLIP, Flamingo).
summary: Existing sequence transduction models rely on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks that are difficult to parallelize. The authors propose the Transformer, a new architecture based solely on attention mechanisms that eliminates recurrence and convolutions. The model achieved a state-of-the-art 28.4 BLEU on English-to-German translation and 41.8 BLEU on English-to-French translation while requiring significantly less training time.

title:
LXMERT: Learning Cross-Modality Encoder Representations from
  Transformers
authors: Hao Tan, Mohit Bansal
reason: A seminal work that introduced the multi-encoder Transformer architecture and diverse pre-training objectives (MLM, cross-modality matching) for VLMs.
summary: To address the challenge of aligning visual concepts with language semantics, the researchers developed LXMERT, a large-scale Transformer framework comprising object relationship, language, and cross-modality encoders. The model was pre-trained on extensive image-sentence pairs using five diverse tasks, including masked language modeling and cross-modality matching. This approach achieved state-of-the-art results on VQA and GQA datasets and improved the previous best performance on the NLVR2 task by 22% absolute (from 54% to 76%).

title: SimVLM: Simple Visual Language Model Pretraining with Weak Supervision
authors:
Zirui Wang, Jiahui Yu, Adams Wei Yu, Zihang Dai, Yulia Tsvetkov, Yuan

reason: Introduces a simplified, single-objective (prefix LM) framework that became a key paradigm for scaling VLM pretraining via weak supervision.
summary: Existing vision-language pretraining methods are often limited by the need for expensive, high-quality annotations and complex, multi-task training objectives. SimVLM addresses this by using a minimalist, end-to-end framework that relies on large-scale weak supervision and a single prefix language modeling objective. This approach achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks, including improvements of 3.74% in VQA score, 1.17% in NLVR2 accuracy, and 10.1% in average CIDEr score for image captioning.

This approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in tasks such as image captioning, visual question-answering, and scene-text understanding.

title:

authors: Wonjae Kim, Bokyung Son, Ildoo Kim

summary: Existing vision-and-language pre-training models are computationally inefficient and limited by their reliance on heavy convolutional architectures and object detection. This approach is up to tens of times faster than previous models while maintaining competitive or superior performance on downstream tasks.

title: VisualBERT: A Simple and Performant Baseline for Vision and Language
authors: Liunian Harold Li, Mark Yatskar, Da Yin, Cho-Jui Hsieh, Kai-Wei Chang

summary: VisualBERT addresses the challenge of modeling complex vision-and-language tasks by integrating text and image regions into a single Transformer-based framework. The method uses a stack of Transformer layers with self-attention to implicitly align linguistic elements with visual regions, pre-trained using two visually-grounded language model objectives. The model achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance across four major tasks (VQA, VCR, NLVR2, and Flickr30K) while maintaining a significantly simpler architecture.

title: FLAVA: A Foundational Language And Vision Alignment Model
authors:

summary: Current vision and language models are often limited to specific modalities or task types, such as being either purely cross-modal or purely multi-modal. The model demonstrates impressive performance across a wide range of 35 different downstream tasks.

title:
MiniGPT-4: Enhancing Vision-Language Understanding with Advanced Large
  Language Models
authors: Deyao Zhu, Jun Chen, Xiaoqian Shen, Xiang Li, Mohamed Elhoseiny
reason: Demonstrates the standard 'frozen encoder + projection layer + frozen LLM' architecture and two-stage training (alignment then instruction tuning).
summary: MiniGPT-4 addresses the lack of advanced multi-modal capabilities in existing vision-language models by aligning a frozen visual encoder with a frozen large language model (Vicuna) using a single projection layer. The researchers utilized a two-stage training process, including a curated detailed image description dataset, to prevent unnatural language outputs like repetition. The method successfully enables emerging multi-modal abilities such as detailed image description, website creation from hand-drawn drafts, and creative storytelling based on visual input.

title:

authors:

The model achieved state-of-the-art zero-shot performance across all tested datasets, outperforming larger models like Flamingo and reaching 90.7% accuracy on the ScienceQA task when fine-tuned.

title: VL-BERT: Pre-training of Generic Visual-Linguistic Representations
authors: Weijie Su, Xizhou Zhu, Yue Cao, Bin Li, Lewei Lu, Furu Wei, Jifeng Dai

The model was pre-trained on the large-scale Conceptual Captions dataset to better align visual and textual information. This approach improved performance across multiple tasks, including visual question answering and visual commonsense reasoning, and achieved first place for a single model on the VCR benchmark leaderboard.

title: VQA: Visual Question Answering
authors:

They introduce a new task and a large-scale dataset consisting of approximately 0.25 million images, 0.76 million questions, and 10 million answers. Feilong Chen, Duzhen Zhang, Minglun Han, Xiuyi Chen, Jing Shi, Shuang
  Xu, Bo Xu
reason: Directly addresses the question by reviewing architectures and pre-training objectives in the vision-language domain.
summary: This paper addresses the challenge of applying pre-training techniques to multi-modal tasks involving both vision and language. The authors provide a comprehensive survey of the field by categorizing recent advances in feature extraction, model architecture, pre-training objectives, datasets, and downstream tasks for both image-text and video-text models. The result is a systematic overview of the current state of vision-language pre-training (VLP) and its emerging research frontiers.

title: VILA: On Pre-training for Visual Language Models
authors:
Ji Lin, Hongxu Yin, Wei Ping, Yao Lu, Pavlo Molchanov, Andrew Tao,
  Huizi Mao, Jan Kautz, Mohammad Shoeybi, Song Han
reason: Analyzes key design choices (freezing LLMs, data types, instruction tuning) for modern VLM pre-training, though not the original seminal work.
summary: This research investigates how different pre-training strategies affect the performance and capabilities of Visual Language Models (VLMs). By testing various configurations, the authors found that unfreezing the LLM is necessary for in-context learning, interleaved data is superior to simple image-text pairs, and re-blending text-only data during fine-tuning prevents performance degradation. The resulting VILA model family consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art models like LLaVA-1.5 across major benchmarks.

title: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
authors:
Hugo Touvron, Thibaut Lavril, Gautier Izacard, Xavier Martinet,
  Marie-Anne Lachaux, Timoth\'ee Lacroix, Baptiste Rozi\`ere, Naman Goyal, Eric
  Hambro, Faisal Azhar, Aurelien Rodriguez, Armand Joulin, Edouard Grave,
  Guillaume Lample
reason: LLaMA is a text-only LLM. While it provides the backbone for many vision-language models (like LLaVA), it is not a vision-language architecture itself.
summary: Researchers sought to develop high-performing foundation language models using only publicly available datasets rather than proprietary data. They trained a collection of models ranging from 7B to 65B parameters on trillions of tokens. The resulting LLaMA-13B model outperformed the much larger GPT-3 (175B) on most benchmarks, while the 65B version proved competitive with leading models like Chinchilla-70B and PaLM-540B.

title: Hierarchical Text-Conditional Image Generation with CLIP Latents
authors: Aditya Ramesh, Prafulla Dhariwal, Alex Nichol, Casey Chu, Mark Chen
reason: Describes the two-stage architecture (prior + decoder) using CLIP latents, a key method for modern text-to-image VLM generation.
summary: This research addresses the difficulty of generating diverse, high-quality images from text by proposing a two-stage hierarchical model that first generates a CLIP image embedding (the prior) and then converts that embedding into a final image (the decoder). By explicitly modeling the CLIP latent space, the method improves image diversity and enables zero-shot language-guided image manipulations. The authors found that using a diffusion model for the prior is more computationally efficient and produces higher-quality samples than autoregressive models.

title: MMBench: Is Your Multi-modal Model an All-around Player?
authors:
Yuan Liu, Haodong Duan, Yuanhan Zhang, Bo Li, Songyang Zhang, Wangbo
  Zhao, Yike Yuan, Jiaqi Wang, Conghui He, Ziwei Liu, Kai Chen, Dahua Lin
reason: This is an evaluation benchmark paper. While it discusses VLMs, it does not introduce foundational architectures or training objectives.
summary: Current vision-language model evaluations lack fine-grained assessment and scalability due to a reliance on limited quantitative metrics or biased human labor. The researchers developed MMBench, a bilingual (English and Chinese) benchmark that uses a "CircularEval" strategy and LLM-assisted conversion of free-form answers into multiple-choice formats to ensure objective and accurate scoring. This systematic pipeline provides a more robust and holistic way to measure diverse multimodal capabilities across different languages.

title: Masked Autoencoders Are Scalable Vision Learners
authors:
Kaiming He, Xinlei Chen, Saining Xie, Yanghao Li, Piotr Doll\'ar, Ross
  Girshick
reason: MAE is a key self-supervised training objective for vision models, though it is primarily a vision-only method rather than vision-language.
summary: To improve the efficiency and scalability of self-supervised vision learning, this paper introduces a Masked Autoencoder (MAE) that uses an asymmetric architecture to reconstruct images from a highly masked input. By masking 75% of an image and processing only the visible patches through the encoder, the method accelerates training by 3x or more. This approach allows a ViT-Huge model to achieve 87.8% accuracy on ImageNet-1K, outperforming supervised pre-training on downstream tasks.

title:
VisionLLM: Large Language Model is also an Open-Ended Decoder for
  Vision-Centric Tasks
authors:
Wenhai Wang, Zhe Chen, Xiaokang Chen, Jiannan Wu, Xizhou Zhu, Gang
  Zeng, Ping Luo, Tong Lu, Jie Zhou, Yu Qiao, Jifeng Dai
reason: Represents recent work in unifying vision tasks via LLM decoders, but is a specific application/extension rather than a foundational architecture.
summary: Current vision foundation models are often limited to pre-defined task formats, lacking the open-ended flexibility of Large Language Models (LLMs). The researchers developed VisionLLM, a framework that treats images as a foreign language and uses an LLM-based decoder to perform vision-centric tasks via flexible language instructions. This approach allows for customizable task granularity and achieves over 60% mAP on the COCO dataset, performing on par with specialized detection models.

title: Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
authors:
Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao and Ji-Rong
  Wen
reason: Focuses on a specific failure mode (hallucination) and evaluation (POPE) rather than the foundational architectures or training objectives.
summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) frequently generate descriptions containing objects that do not exist in the target images, a phenomenon known as object hallucination. This study systematically investigates this issue across representative models and identifies that hallucinations are often triggered by objects mentioned in visual instructions or those that frequently co-occur with image content. To address the instability of existing metrics, the researchers propose POPE, a polling-based query method that provides a more stable and flexible way to evaluate object hallucination.

title: Multimodal Few-Shot Learning with Frozen Language Models
authors:
Maria Tsimpoukelli, Jacob Menick, Serkan Cabi, S. M. Ali Eslami, Oriol

reason: Introduces the paradigm of using frozen LLMs with visual prefix tuning, a key architectural pattern for modern multimodal models.
summary: This research addresses the challenge of transferring the few-shot learning capabilities of large language models to multimodal tasks involving both vision and text. The authors train a vision encoder to convert images into continuous embeddings that act as prefixes for a frozen, pre-trained language model. The resulting system successfully performs new tasks, such as learning novel object names and visual question-answering, by processing interleaved sequences of image and text examples.

title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
authors: Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, Jian Sun
reason: ResNets are a foundational vision architecture used as backbones in many early and modern vision-language models, though not a VLM itself.
summary: Training very deep neural networks is difficult because they are hard to optimize. The researchers introduced a residual learning framework that reformulates layers to learn residual functions instead of unreferenced ones. This approach allowed for networks up to 152 layers deep, achieving a 3.57% error rate on the ImageNet test set and winning first place in several 2015 visual recognition competitions.

title:
VLMo: Unified Vision-Language Pre-Training with
  Mixture-of-Modality-Experts
authors:
Hangbo Bao, Wenhui Wang, Li Dong, Qiang Liu, Owais Khan Mohammed,
  Kriti Aggarwal, Subhojit Som, Furu Wei
reason: Introduces a modular architecture (MoME) and unified pre-training strategy that bridges dual and fusion encoders, a key concept in modern VLMs.
summary: To address the need for a single model capable of both efficient image-text retrieval and complex vision-language reasoning, researchers developed VLMo, a modular Transformer architecture using a Mixture-of-Modality-Experts (MoME) approach. This method utilizes modality-specific experts and a stagewise pre-training strategy to learn both dual-encoder and fusion-encoder capabilities simultaneously. VLMo achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks, including VQA, NLVR2, and image-text retrieval tasks.

title:
LAION-5B: An open large-scale dataset for training next generation
  image-text models
authors:

reason: The paper focuses on a dataset rather than the architectures or training objectives themselves, though it enables their training.
summary: To democratize research on large-scale multimodal models, the authors released LAION-5B, an open dataset containing 5.85 billion CLIP-filtered image-text pairs, including 2.32 billion in English. The dataset was used to successfully replicate and fine-tune foundational models such as CLIP, GLIDE, and Stable Diffusion. The release also includes tools for dataset exploration, subset generation, and content filtering for watermarks, NSFW, and toxicity.

title:
Flickr30k Entities: Collecting Region-to-Phrase Correspondences for
  Richer Image-to-Sentence Models
authors:
Bryan A. Plummer, Liwei Wang, Chris M. Cervantes, Juan C. Caicedo,
  Julia Hockenmaier, and Svetlana Lazebnik
reason: Focuses on dataset augmentation and grounding (localization) rather than the core architectures/objectives of modern VLMs like CLIP/ALM.
summary: Current image-to-sentence models lack fine-grained connections between specific words and their locations in an image. The researchers created the Flickr30k Entities dataset, which adds 244k coreference chains and 276k manually annotated bounding boxes to the existing Flickr30k captions. While their baseline model successfully localizes textual entities, they found that these localization improvements do not automatically translate to better performance in image-sentence retrieval tasks.

title: MME: A Comprehensive Evaluation Benchmark for Multimodal Large Language Models
authors: Chaoyou Fu, Peixian Chen, Yunhang Shen, Yulei Qin, Mengdan Zhang, Xu Lin, Jinrui Yang, Xiawu Zheng, Ke Li, Xing Sun, Yunsheng Wu, Rongrong Ji, Caifeng Shan, Ran He
reason: This is an evaluation benchmark paper. While it assesses MLLMs, it does not introduce the foundational architectures or training objectives.
summary: Current evaluation methods for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) lack comprehensiveness and are prone to data leakage. The researchers developed MME, a benchmark consisting of 14 manually annotated subtasks designed to measure both perception and cognition across various multimodal tasks. Testing 30 advanced MLLMs revealed that existing models still have significant room for improvement and identified specific directions for future optimization.

title: BEiT: BERT Pre-Training of Image Transformers
authors: Hangbo Bao, Li Dong, Songhao Piao, Furu Wei
reason: Introduces masked image modeling (MIM) for ViTs, a key training objective used in many modern vision-language pre-training pipelines.
summary: To improve vision Transformer pre-training, researchers developed BEiT, a self-supervised method that uses a masked image modeling task similar to BERT in natural language processing. The model learns by masking image patches and attempting to recover discrete visual tokens through a backbone Transformer. This approach achieves 83.2% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K for the base model, outperforming from-scratch DeiT training (81.8%), and reaches 86.3% for the large model.

title:
Learn to Explain: Multimodal Reasoning via Thought Chains for Science
  Question Answering
authors:
Pan Lu, Swaroop Mishra, Tony Xia, Liang Qiu, Kai-Wei Chang, Song-Chun
  Zhu, Oyvind Tafjord, Peter Clark, Ashwin Kalyan
reason: Focuses on a specific reasoning task (CoT) and benchmark (ScienceQA) rather than the foundational architectures or training objectives of VLMs.
summary: Existing science question-answering benchmarks lack multimodal diversity and annotated reasoning processes, such as lectures and explanations. The researchers introduced ScienceQA, a new dataset of approximately 21,000 multimodal multiple-choice questions, and trained models to use these annotations as a chain-of-thought reasoning process. The results show that using these explanations improves few-shot GPT-3 performance by 18.96% and allows models to achieve the same performance using only 40% of the training data.

title: Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows
authors:
Ze Liu and Yutong Lin and Yue Cao and Han Hu and Yixuan Wei and Zheng
  Zhang and Stephen Lin and Baining Guo
reason: Swin is a major vision backbone used in many VLMs, but it is a vision-only architecture, not a vision-language model itself.
summary: Standard Vision Transformers struggle with high-resolution images due to the high computational cost of global self-attention. The Swin Transformer addresses this by using a hierarchical architecture with a shifted window scheme that limits attention to local, non-overlapping windows while maintaining cross-window connections. This method achieves linear computational complexity and sets new state-of-the-art results, including 87.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K and 58.7 box AP on COCO.

title: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context
authors:
Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross
  Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr
  Doll\'ar
reason: While COCO is a cornerstone dataset for vision tasks, it is a data resource rather than an architecture or training objective for VLM models.
summary: Current object recognition datasets lack the complex, real-world context necessary for true scene understanding. Researchers created the Microsoft COCO dataset by collecting 328,000 images containing 2.5 million labeled instances across 91 object categories, using per-instance segmentations to improve localization. This dataset provides a more challenging benchmark for bounding box and segmentation tasks compared to previous datasets like PASCAL and ImageNet.

title:
Pixel-BERT: Aligning Image Pixels with Text by Deep Multi-Modal
  Transformers
authors: Zhicheng Huang, Zhaoyang Zeng, Bei Liu, Dongmei Fu, Jianlong Fu
reason: Introduces pixel-level alignment and specific pre-training objectives (MLM, ITM) used in modern VLMs, though post-dates the very first foundational works.
summary: Pixel-BERT addresses the limitations of region-based visual features by directly aligning image pixels with text semantics using a unified, end-to-end multi-modal transformer. The method utilizes random pixel sampling alongside Masked Language Modeling and Image-Text Matching pre-training tasks on the Visual Genome and MS-COCO datasets. This approach achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple downstream tasks, including a 2.17 point improvement in Visual Question Answering (VQA) performance compared to previous models.

title:
Making the V in VQA Matter: Elevating the Role of Image Understanding in
  Visual Question Answering
authors: Yash Goyal, Tejas Khot, Douglas Summers-Stay, Dhruv Batra, Devi Parikh
reason: Focuses on dataset bias and VQA evaluation rather than proposing foundational architectures or training objectives for VLMs.
summary: Current Visual Question Answering (VQA) models often rely on language biases rather than actual visual understanding, leading to inflated performance metrics. To address this, the researchers created the VQA v2.0 dataset by pairing each question with two similar images that require different answers, effectively doubling the number of image-question pairs. Benchmarking shows that state-of-the-art models perform significantly worse on this balanced dataset, providing empirical evidence that they have been exploiting language priors instead of visual cues.

title: MM-Vet: Evaluating Large Multimodal Models for Integrated Capabilities
authors:
Weihao Yu, Zhengyuan Yang, Linjie Li, Jianfeng Wang, Kevin Lin,
  Zicheng Liu, Xinchao Wang, Lijuan Wang
reason: This is an evaluation benchmark for existing models, not a paper describing foundational architectures or training objectives.
summary: MM-Vet addresses the difficulty of evaluating large multimodal models on complex, integrated tasks that require combining multiple core vision-language capabilities. The researchers developed a benchmark consisting of 16 different capability combinations and an LLM-based evaluator to provide unified scoring for open-ended responses. This method allows for a systematic assessment of how well models integrate diverse skills, such as mathematical reasoning and visual joke explanation, beyond simple performance rankings.

title:
Bottom-Up and Top-Down Attention for Image Captioning and Visual
  Question Answering
authors:
Peter Anderson, Xiaodong He, Chris Buehler, Damien Teney, Mark

reason: Introduced the bottom-up/top-down attention paradigm (using object detectors) which was a precursor to modern modular VLM architectures.
summary: This research addresses the limitations of standard visual attention in image captioning and visual question answering by combining bottom-up object detection with top-down feature weighting. The method uses a Faster R-CNN to propose salient image regions and then applies a top-down mechanism to weight these features for reasoning. This approach achieved state-of-the-art results on MSCOCO with CIDEr, SPICE, and BLEU-4 scores of 117.9, 21.5, and 36.9, respectively, and secured first place in the 2017 VQA Challenge.

title:
GQA: A New Dataset for Real-World Visual Reasoning and Compositional
  Question Answering
authors: Drew A. Hudson and Christopher D. Manning
reason: Focuses on a specific dataset and reasoning task (VQA) rather than the foundational architectures or training objectives of VLMs.
summary: Existing Visual Question Answering (VQA) datasets often lack the complexity required for true visual reasoning and are prone to dataset biases. The researchers developed GQA, a dataset of 22 million diverse questions generated via a scene graph-based engine that uses functional programs to control answer distributions and mitigate bias. While human performance reaches 89.3%, current state-of-the-art VQA models achieve only 54.1%, highlighting a significant gap in compositional reasoning capabilities.

title:
Large-Scale Adversarial Training for Vision-and-Language Representation
  Learning
authors: Zhe Gan, Yen-Chun Chen, Linjie Li, Chen Zhu, Yu Cheng, Jingjing Liu
reason: Introduces adversarial training as a method to improve V+L representations, building on existing architectures to enhance robustness and invariance.
summary: Vision-and-language models often lack robustness due to vulnerabilities in their representation learning. The researchers developed VILLA, a two-stage training method that applies "free" adversarial perturbations directly to the embedding spaces of images and text rather than raw pixels or tokens. This approach achieved new state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks, including Visual Question Answering, Image-Text Retrieval, and Visual Entailment.

title:
MMMU: A Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning
  Benchmark for Expert AGI
authors:

summary: Current multimodal models struggle to perform complex reasoning tasks that require specialized, college-level subject knowledge across diverse visual formats. Researchers developed MMMU, a benchmark containing 11.5K questions spanning 30 subjects and 183 subfields, including complex images like chemical structures and music sheets. Testing revealed a significant performance gap, as even leading models like GPT-4V and Gemini Ultra achieved only 56% and 59% accuracy, respectively.

title:
Multi-Grained Vision Language Pre-Training: Aligning Texts with Visual
  Concepts
authors: Yan Zeng, Xinsong Zhang, Hang Li
reason: Introduces multi-grained alignment (object/concept level) which is a key evolution in VLM training objectives beyond global image-text matching.
summary: Current vision-language pre-training methods struggle to model relationships between multiple objects because they rely too heavily on isolated, object-centric features. X-VLM addresses this by implementing multi-grained alignment, which locates specific visual concepts within an image to link them with corresponding text at various levels of granularity. This approach consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across multiple downstream vision-language tasks.

title: Foundational Models Defining a New Era in Vision: A Survey and Outlook
authors:
Muhammad Awais, Muzammal Naseer, Salman Khan, Rao Muhammad Anwer,
  Hisham Cholakkal, Mubarak Shah, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Fahad Shahbaz Khan
reason: Comprehensive survey covering architectures and training objectives (contrastive, generative) specifically for vision-language foundational models.
summary: Current vision systems struggle to reason about complex, multi-modal visual scenes and their compositional relationships. This survey reviews the architectures, training objectives, and prompting mechanisms of emerging foundational models that bridge vision with text, audio, and depth. The paper identifies critical research gaps in the field, including challenges in real-world understanding, evaluation benchmarking, and vulnerability to adversarial attacks.

title: Grounding Language Models to Images for Multimodal Inputs and Outputs
authors: Jing Yu Koh, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, Daniel Fried
reason: Describes a key method for grounding frozen LLMs to vision via linear layers, a common architectural pattern in modern VLMs (e.g., Flamingo style).
summary: This research addresses the challenge of enabling text-only language models to process and generate interleaved sequences of text and images. The authors propose keeping a pretrained language model frozen while fine-tuning only the input and output linear layers to facilitate cross-modality interaction. This method achieves strong zero-shot performance on tasks such as contextual image retrieval and multimodal dialogue.

The researchers developed u-LLaVA, a framework that integrates pixel, regional, and global features through a joint instruction tuning method using task-specific projectors and decoders. This approach achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks using a new mask-based multi-task dataset containing 277,000 samples.

title:
MMCOMPOSITION: Revisiting the Compositionality of Pre-trained
  Vision-Language Models
authors:
Hang Hua, Yunlong Tang, Ziyun Zeng, Liangliang Cao, Zhengyuan Yang,
  Hangfeng He, Chenliang Xu, Jiebo Luo
reason: Focuses on evaluating compositionality in existing VLMs rather than defining the foundational architectures or training objectives themselves.
summary: Current vision-language models (VLMs) lack a comprehensive evaluation of their ability to understand novel combinations of visual and textual components, particularly regarding complex object interactions and counting. The researchers introduced MMCOMPOSITION, a new human-annotated benchmark designed to measure fine-grained compositional perception and reasoning. Their analysis reveals that mainstream models struggle with these tasks, with GPT-4o surprisingly performing worse in compositionality than the top-performing open-source model.

title:
Contrastive Vision-Language Alignment Makes Efficient Instruction
  Learner
authors:
Lizhao Liu, Xinyu Sun, Tianhang Xiang, Zhuangwei Zhuang, Liuren Yin,
  Mingkui Tan
reason: Discusses specific alignment objectives (contrastive vs generative) for instruction tuning, but is an optimization of existing VLM paradigms.
summary: Existing methods for extending large language models to vision-language tasks rely on generative captioning losses that result in weak alignment and high data requirements. The researchers propose CG-VLM, which combines generative and contrastive objectives by maximizing the similarity between pooled image-patch features and text-token embeddings. This approach enables efficient learning, achieving 95% of the performance of the state-of-the-art LLaVA model on the zero-shot ScienceQA-Image benchmark using only 10% of the instruction tuning data.

title: 3VL: Using Trees to Improve Vision-Language Models' Interpretability
authors: Nir Yellinek, Leonid Karlinsky and Raja Giryes
reason: Proposes a specific architectural modification (tree-augmented) to improve compositional reasoning and interpretability in VLMs.
summary: Vision-language models often struggle to understand compositional concepts like object attributes and relations, and they lack the interpretability needed to debug these failures. The researchers introduced 3VL, an architecture that incorporates hierarchical tree structures into visual representations, alongside the Anchor inference method and the DiRe interpretability tool. This approach improves compositional reasoning performance on the VL-Checklist benchmark and provides visual explanations for why a model succeeds or fails.

title: MMRL: Multi-Modal Representation Learning for Vision-Language Models
authors: Yuncheng Guo, Xiaodong Gu
reason: Focuses on a specific adaptation/regularization technique for few-shot transfer, rather than the foundational architectures/objectives.
summary: Adapting large-scale vision-language models to new tasks with limited data often causes overfitting and poor generalization. The MMRL framework addresses this by introducing a shared, modality-agnostic representation space that optimizes both class and representation tokens at higher encoder layers while using a regularization term to align features with the original zero-shot model. Across 15 datasets, this method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches by effectively balancing task-specific adaptation with the preservation of generalized knowledge.

title: Challenges and Prospects in Vision and Language Research
authors: Kushal Kafle, Robik Shrestha, Christopher Kanan
reason: A review of the state of vision-language tasks in 2019; provides context on the field's evolution but doesn't define the modern architectures.
summary: Current vision-language models often achieve high scores by exploiting dataset flaws and evaluation loopholes rather than demonstrating true integrated reasoning. This paper reviews these systemic weaknesses and proposes a new framework for developing more robust, capability-driven benchmarks. The goal is to move beyond superficial performance metrics toward tasks that genuinely test the intersection of vision, reasoning, and language.
